title: Coasteering in Anglesey
strapline: Leap into adventure along Anglesey's dramatic coast – no wetsuit required (but highly recommended!).
metaDescription: Explore Anglesey's stunning coastline with exhilarating coasteering routes. Find the best spots, guided tours, and gear for your adventure!
heroAlt: Coasteerers jumping off a rocky cliff into the sea in Anglesey
introduction:
Anglesey, or Ynys Môn as we call it, is a coasteering paradise. Forget generic beaches; here, you'll find towering sea cliffs, hidden coves, and crystal-clear waters teeming with marine life. What sets Anglesey apart from other Welsh coasteering destinations is the sheer variety. You can find sheltered bays perfect for beginners, or exposed headlands that will challenge even the most experienced adrenaline junkies. 

The geological diversity is stunning. Imagine scrambling over ancient volcanic rock at South Stack, then swimming through sea caves carved into limestone near Rhoscolyn. The water clarity is exceptional, especially on a sunny day, giving you unparalleled views of the underwater world. You might even spot a seal or two! 

Coasteering Anglesey is fantastic for families looking for a unique holiday experience, groups of friends seeking adventure, or solo thrill-seekers wanting to push their limits. However, let's be honest, it's not always sunshine and rainbows. The sea can be unpredictable, and some routes are exposed to strong currents and swells. Always check the weather forecast and tide times before you go, and if you're unsure, book a guided tour with a reputable operator. 

Compared to Pembrokeshire, Anglesey's coasteering routes tend to be a bit more technical, requiring a slightly higher level of fitness and scrambling ability. But the rewards are worth it – the sense of accomplishment after completing a challenging route, the breathtaking views, and the feeling of truly connecting with nature. The vibrant coastal communities also offer excellent post-coasteering refuelling options from cosy cafes to excellent restaurants. Don't forget to bring your camera (waterproof, of course!) to capture the memories.
topTips: South Stack Cliffs is closed to coasteering during parts of the bird nesting season – check the RSPB South Stack website before you plan a trip, as exclusion zones on this stretch of coast can run from spring into autumn some years.

Trearddur Bay has genuine rip currents, not just theoretical ones – the RNLI Trearddur Bay lifeboat station has rescued swimmers and bodyboarders caught in rip tides here as recently as September 2025 and February 2026. Stick to the smaller coves north of the main beach and never coasteer alone.

Arrive early. Porth Dafarch's car park fills up fast in summer, and Rhoscolyn and Cable Bay both only have small car parks – if you're not there by mid-morning in July or August, expect to be parking in the village and walking down.

Most operators won't take under-8s coasteering, and full-day or 'adventure' sessions are often restricted to 14+. If you're bringing younger kids, book a half-day or 'eco' session and check the specific operator's age policy before you commit.

You don't need to book a guide to coasteer in Anglesey, but if you're new to it, do. Sheltered spots like Church Bay and Porth Dafarch are genuinely fine for a self-led first go in calm conditions; South Stack and Cable Bay are not the place to learn currents and swell on your own.
Check the surf and swell forecast the morning of your session, not the night before. Cable Bay in particular can flip from fun and mellow to genuinely dangerous if a swell picks up.
Wetsuits are worth having even in August. Anglesey's sea stays cold well into summer, and most of these routes involve long swims between jumps, not just the odd dip.

Book post-coasteering food ahead in peak season – the Lobster Pot in Church Bay and The White Eagle in Rhoscolyn are both small and popular, and turning up dripping wet on a Saturday evening without a table is a common rookie mistake.

firstTimer: Start at a sheltered spot. Church Bay (Porth Swtan) or Porth Dafarch are the easiest introductions – lower cliffs, calmer water, and shorter sessions – before you attempt anything at South Stack or Cable Bay.
You need to be a confident swimmer, not just an okay one. You should be able to swim in open water and tread water for a while – a buoyancy aid helps, but it isn't a substitute for swimming ability.
Full kit matters: wetsuit, buoyancy aid, helmet, coasteering shoes, and gloves. Hire from Anglesey Adventures or Anglesey Outdoors in Llanfairpwllgwyngyll if you don't own gear.

Book a guided session for your first time at anything graded 'Moderate' or above. South Stack, Rhoscolyn, Trearddur Bay and Cable Bay all have currents, swell, and submerged rocks that aren't obvious from the shore.

Check the tide times before you go, not just the weather. Several of these bays (Church Bay, Aberffraw) change character completely between high and low tide, and access to some scrambles is tide-dependent.
Tell someone your plan – which cove, what time you're going in, when you expect to be out. If something goes wrong, dial 999 or 112 and ask for the Coastguard.
Don't coasteer during or right after a big swell, even at the 'easy' spots. Check a surf/swell forecast for the area – Cable Bay's surf report is a good proxy for west-coast conditions generally.
Bring warm layers and a hot drink for afterwards. You'll be colder than you expect once you're out of the water, even in summer.
regular: Skip the honeypots on a sunny Saturday. Trearddur Bay and Rhoscolyn get busy fast – Church Bay and Porth Dafarch are quieter, and the smaller coves north of Trearddur's main beach are usually empty even when the main bay is packed.

Aberffraw and the Inish Mon (Ynys Môn) National Nature Reserve stretch are the pick for solitude – longer approach, less foot traffic, and proper wildlife (seals, seabirds) if you're patient and stick to established routes.

May and late September are the sweet spot: water's warming up (or hasn't cooled yet), the RSPB nesting restrictions at South Stack have usually lifted or not yet started, and the summer crowds are gone.
Keep an eye on the RSPB South Stack updates through spring – nesting closures move year to year, and a route that was open last May might not be this year.

If Cable Bay's swell is too big to coasteer, it's usually still rideable as a surf spot – check conditions before you drive out, since the same swell that ruins coasteering can make the detour worthwhile for a surf instead.

Combine two spots in a day if you're experienced: Porth Dafarch or Church Bay in the morning for an easy warm-up swim, then South Stack or Rhoscolyn in the afternoon once you've got a feel for the day's conditions.
Walk the coastal path south from Aberffraw beach for quieter rock formations away from the main access point – most visitors don't go further than the first few hundred metres.
For a low-key finish, the Wavecrest Café and Sea Shanty Café in Trearddur Bay are far less likely to have a wait than the sit-down restaurants, and they're both right on the sand.

spots.name: South Stack Cliffs
spots.description: A classic Anglesey coasteering spot with dramatic cliffs, caves, and challenging jumps. Expect exhilarating swims in crystal-clear water and the chance to spot nesting seabirds. Be mindful of the tides as this is a very exposed location.
spots.bestFor: Experienced coasteerers looking for a thrill
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those with a fear of heights
spots.parking: Large National Trust car park at South Stack (LL65 1YH), £5 for non-members. Arrive early in peak season.
spots.insiderTip: Check the RSPB website for bird nesting season closures. The cliffs are closed to coasteering at certain times of the year to protect nesting birds.
spots.howToDoIt: Sessions typically start with a briefing and kit check at the car park, then a walk down to a sheltered entry point below the lighthouse before working along the base of the cliffs. Expect a mix of deep-water jumps (some from height), swims between rock platforms, and short scrambles over volcanic rock – this is not a route to attempt without recent coasteering experience or a guide, given the exposure and depth of water involved.
spots.access: Access is via the South Stack road and the National Trust car park; from there it's a walk down towards the lighthouse steps before dropping onto the coasteering entry points. This stretch sits within an RSPB reserve, so check current nesting-season restrictions before you go – access can be closed or limited during breeding season. Tides and swell matter more here than almost anywhere else on this list; this is an exposed, open-water stretch of coast.
spots.routeDescription: A committing line beneath South Stack's cliffs, threading between sea stacks and into small caves before reaching the main jump platforms. The rock is old volcanic rhyolite, sharp in places, and the water is deep close to shore – jumps here range from a few metres to genuinely high, operator-guided leaps. Seabirds nest directly above the route in season, so expect noise, guano, and (rightly) restricted access at certain times of year.

spots.name: Rhoscolyn Headland
spots.description: A popular spot with a mix of jumps, swims, and scrambling. The rock formations are incredible, and the water is usually calm and clear. This route offers good views of the coastline and is suitable for a range of abilities.
spots.parking: Small car park near Rhoscolyn beach (LL65 2QQ). Can get busy in summer.
spots.insiderTip: Head to The White Eagle pub after your coasteer for some well-deserved food and drinks – it's a local favourite.
spots.howToDoIt: Groups usually enter from the beach and work out along the headland, mixing rock-hopping and scrambling with a string of jumps of varying heights and a couple of longer swims between platforms. It's a good route for building confidence – there are usually easier alternatives alongside the bigger jumps, so you can opt in or out of the scarier features as you go.
spots.access: Park at the small car park near Rhoscolyn beach (fills quickly in summer – if it's full, the village has some roadside parking with a short walk down) and access the water directly from the beach. The headland route is exposed to swell from the west, so it's worth checking conditions before committing to the full route rather than staying in the sheltered bay.
spots.routeDescription: A varied line around the Rhoscolyn headland taking in gullies, natural rock arches, and a series of jumps from ledges of different heights, connected by swims across clear, sheltered water. The rock formations here are some of the most striking on this list, and the going is generally calmer than South Stack or Cable Bay, making it a solid step up from a first-timer route.

spots.name: Church Bay (Porth Swtan)
spots.description: A more sheltered bay with a pebble beach and lower cliffs. This is a good option for beginners or those looking for a less challenging experience. The water is often calm, and there are plenty of rock pools to explore.
spots.bestFor: Families with young children and beginner coasteerers
spots.parking: Car park right next to Church Bay beach (LL65 4EU). Parking fee applies.
spots.insiderTip: Visit the Lobster Pot café for delicious seafood after your coasteering adventure. They also have great ice cream!
spots.howToDoIt: A gentle introduction: enter from the pebble beach, work along the low cliffs at the bay's edges exploring rock pools and small gullies, with a handful of low jumps into calm water. Well suited to a self-led session in settled conditions if you're not ready to book a guide, though a guided session is still the safer choice with young children.
spots.access: Park at the car park right next to the beach (a parking fee applies) and walk straight onto the sand. The bay is at its best at low-to-mid tide, when the beach is widest and the rock pools are exposed; at high tide, the sheltered scrambling area shrinks considerably, so time your visit around the tide table rather than just the forecast.
spots.routeDescription: A short, low-commitment route hugging the low cliffs either side of the pebble beach, with plenty of rock pools to explore between features. There's little in the way of serious jumps or swims here – it's more coastal exploration than adrenaline, which is exactly why it works well for families and nervous first-timers.

spots.name: Trearddur Bay
spots.description: A popular tourist spot with several small beaches and rocky outcrops. Offers a mix of easy scrambling and some more challenging jumps. Good for families but can be very busy during peak season.
spots.parking: Multiple car parks in Trearddur Bay (LL65 2YW). Charges apply.
spots.insiderTip: Explore the smaller coves to the north of the main beach for quieter coasteering spots.
spots.howToDoIt: Routes typically start from one of the smaller coves rather than the main beach, working across rocky outcrops with a mix of easy scrambling and a few bigger jumps for those who want them. Given the RNLI's rip current call-outs here, this is a spot where booking a guide who knows the local water is worth the money rather than a nice-to-have.
spots.access: Multiple pay-and-display car parks serve Trearddur Bay; the smaller coves to the north are a short walk from the main beach car parks. Be aware this beach has a documented rip current risk – the RNLI Trearddur Bay lifeboat station has responded to multiple rescues here, including bodyboarders and swimmers caught in rip tides. Stay well clear of the main bay's rip zone and avoid entering the water if red flags or lifeguard warnings are up.
spots.routeDescription: A patchwork of small beaches and rocky headlands strung along Trearddur Bay, offering easy scrambling for most of the route with a few punchier jumps on the rockier sections. The quieter coves north of the main beach have better rock features and far fewer people than the central bay, which is worth the extra five-minute walk.

spots.name: Aberffraw Dunes & Coast
spots.description: A longer stretch of coastline with a mix of sandy beaches, rocky sections, and small cliffs. The estuary offers calmer waters. Involves some walking and wading.
spots.bestFor: Those wanting a longer adventure with varied terrain
spots.notSuitableFor: Those with limited mobility or those looking for high jumps
spots.parking: Car park in Aberffraw village (LL63 5YX), a short walk to the beach.
spots.insiderTip: Walk along the coastal path further south from the main beach to find quieter spots and more interesting rock formations.
spots.howToDoIt: This is more of a coastal expedition than a classic coasteering circuit – expect a longer walk-in, sections of wading and swimming across the estuary mouth, and lower-key scrambling over rocky sections rather than big jumps. Plan for the extra time this involves and bring more supplies than you would for a shorter session.
spots.access: Park in the village car park and walk to the beach; the estuary crossing point is tide-dependent, so check tide times before setting out – attempting the wade at the wrong state of tide can mean a much longer, colder crossing than expected. The Wales Coast Path runs along this stretch, giving a walkable bail-out option if conditions turn.
spots.routeDescription: A longer, more varied stretch than most Anglesey coasteering routes, combining sandy beach, estuary wading, and rocky sections with small cliffs further along the coast. Better suited to those wanting a half-day adventure over pure adrenaline – the appeal here is the terrain variety and relative solitude, not big jumps.

spots.name: Porth Dafarch
spots.description: A sheltered cove, popular with swimmers and divers. Good for a shorter, easier coasteering experience. Offers easy access to the water and some gentle scrambling.
spots.parking: Car park at Porth Dafarch beach (LL65 2LR).
spots.insiderTip: Arrive early in summer, as the car park fills up quickly. Combine your coasteer with a swim in the bay.
spots.howToDoIt: Entry is straight off the beach into a sheltered cove, with easy scrambling around the rocky sides of the bay and a few modest jumps. A good spot to practise the basics – reading the water, timing jumps, moving over wet rock – before stepping up to a more exposed route elsewhere on the island.
spots.access: Small car park directly at the beach; it fills quickly on sunny days, so arrive early or expect to park further up the lane and walk down. The cove is naturally sheltered from most swell directions, which is what makes it reliable for beginners even when other spots are blown out.
spots.routeDescription: A compact, sheltered loop around Porth Dafarch's cove – low rock ledges for scrambling, a couple of easy jump points, and clear water that's also popular with divers and snorkellers. Short enough to combine with a second, more challenging spot later in the day.

spots.name: Cable Bay (Porth Llechog)
spots.description: Known for its surfing, Cable Bay also offers some decent coasteering opportunities. The cliffs are relatively low, but there are some fun jumps and scrambles to be had. Strong currents can be present.
spots.parking: Small car park at Cable Bay (LL65 2NJ).
spots.insiderTip: Check the surf report before you go. If the waves are big, coasteering can be dangerous.
spots.howToDoIt: Enter from the beach and work along the low cliffs either side of the bay, mixing scrambling with a handful of decent jumps. Because this is also a surf break, always check the swell before you go – what makes it fun for surfers can make it genuinely hazardous for coasteering, with surge and current around the rocks picking up fast.
spots.access: Small car park at Cable Bay itself, limited spaces. Check a surf/swell forecast (Magicseaweed's Rhoscolyn report is a reasonable proxy for this stretch of west coast) before setting out – if there's a swell running, treat this as a surf spot, not a coasteering one.
spots.routeDescription: A short but punchy route along Cable Bay's low cliffs, with fun scrambling and a mix of small and larger jumps depending on the swell. Best in calm, settled conditions; give it a miss entirely if there's any meaningful swell forecast.

spots.name: Inish Mon National Nature Reserve
spots.description: This remote and relatively untamed coastal strip offers coasteering opportunities with a twist: stunning flora and fauna. The location offers lots of seals, coastal birds and plant life to view while you scramble. Check local permissions before entering any protected areas.
spots.bestFor: Nature lovers and experienced coasteerers who respect the environment
spots.notSuitableFor: Those who don't take care of the environment or stick to the marked trail.!
spots.parking: Limited parking at the reserve entrance. (LL73 8PH)
spots.insiderTip: Stay on the established routes to minimise damage to the fragile ecosystem. Bring binoculars to spot seals and seabirds.
spots.howToDoIt: This is a slower, nature-focused session rather than a jump-heavy adrenaline route – expect gentle scrambling along the shoreline, some easy swims, and plenty of stops to watch wildlife. Because it's a protected reserve, stick to established access points and don't treat it as a place to push technical or high-jump lines.
spots.access: Limited parking at the reserve entrance – check local permissions and any seasonal access restrictions before you go, as protected nature reserves on Anglesey can have wildlife-driven closures similar to South Stack. Stay on marked routes to avoid damaging the reserve's habitat.
spots.routeDescription: A quieter, wilder stretch of coast than the main tourist spots, with an emphasis on the surrounding flora and fauna as much as the coasteering itself. Seals and coastal birds are a regular sight if you move quietly and stick to the established line rather than exploring off-route.

practicalInfo.weather: The weather in Anglesey can be unpredictable, so it's essential to check the forecast before you go coasteering. Strong winds, heavy rain, and large swells can make conditions dangerous. Sea temperatures are coldest in winter and warmest in late summer, but wetsuits are recommended year-round.
gearChecklist: Wetsuit – essential for warmth and buoyancy
Buoyancy aid – provides extra flotation and visibility
Helmet – protects your head from impacts
Coasteering shoes – grippy footwear for scrambling over rocks
Gloves – protect your hands from scrapes and cold
Waterproof camera – to capture the memories
Towel and warm clothes – for after your coasteering session
Dry bag – to keep your valuables safe and dry
Sunscreen – even on cloudy days, the sun can be strong

gettingThere.publicTransport: Regular train services to Holyhead, with bus connections to other parts of the island. The T5 bus route connects Bangor with Holyhead and serves many coastal villages.
gettingThere.parkingTips: Parking can be limited, especially during peak season. Arrive early or consider using public transport. Be respectful of local residents and avoid parking in restricted areas.

practicalInfo.safety:
Coasteering can be a dangerous activity. Always check the weather forecast and tide times before you go. Never coasteer alone and inform someone of your plans. Be aware of potential hazards such as strong currents, slippery rocks, and submerged objects. If in doubt, book a guided tour with a qualified instructor. 

Emergency: Dial 999 or 112 and ask for the Coastguard.

faqs.question: What is the best time of year to go coasteering in Anglesey?
faqs.answer: The best time for coasteering in Anglesey is between May and October. The sea is warmer, and the weather is generally more settled. However, always check the forecast before you go, as conditions can change quickly.

faqs.question: Do I need to be a strong swimmer to go coasteering?
faqs.answer: Yes, a good level of swimming ability is essential for coasteering. You should be able to swim confidently in open water and be comfortable treading water for extended periods. A buoyancy aid will help, but it's not a substitute for swimming skills.

faqs.question: What should I wear for coasteering?
faqs.answer: A wetsuit, buoyancy aid, helmet, and coasteering shoes are essential. Gloves are also recommended to protect your hands. Layers of thermal clothing can be worn under the wetsuit for extra warmth.

faqs.question: Is coasteering suitable for children?
faqs.answer: Coasteering can be suitable for children, but it depends on their age, swimming ability, and confidence levels. Some routes are more challenging than others, so choose a suitable location and consider booking a guided tour with an experienced instructor.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to go coasteering in Anglesey?
faqs.answer: Coasteering in Anglesey can be free if you have your own gear and know what you're doing. However, guided tours typically cost between £50 and £80 per person. Gear hire is also available from some operators.

faqs.question: What happens if I get into trouble while coasteering?
faqs.answer: If you get into trouble while coasteering, call 999 or 112 and ask for the Coastguard. Stay calm and try to attract attention. If you are with a group, assist each other.

faqs.question: Can I go coasteering if I'm pregnant?
faqs.answer: Coasteering is not recommended during pregnancy due to the physical demands and potential risks involved.

faqs.question: Are there any age restrictions for coasteering?
faqs.answer: Age restrictions vary depending on the operator and the specific route. Generally, children under the age of 8 are not permitted to coasteer. Check with the operator for their specific age restrictions.

postActivitySpots.name: The Oyster Catcher

postActivitySpots.name: Wavecrest Cafe
postActivitySpots.description: A traditional seaside cafe serving breakfast, lunch, and snacks. A popular spot for families and beachgoers. Ideal for a quick and affordable refuel after coasteering.

postActivitySpots.name: Lobster Pot
postActivitySpots.description: A charming tea room and restaurant specializing in fresh lobster and seafood. A must-visit for seafood lovers. Offers stunning views of Church Bay.

postActivitySpots.name: The White Eagle
postActivitySpots.description: A popular gastropub with a relaxed atmosphere and stunning views of the coastline. Serves excellent pub fare and a wide selection of local ales. A great spot to unwind after a day of coasteering.

postActivitySpots.name: The Sea Shanty Cafe
postActivitySpots.description: A cosy cafe right on the beach in Trearddur Bay, offering breakfast, lunch and stunning views. Perfect for a quick bite or a longer stop to watch the waves.

postActivitySpots.name: Sosban & The Secret Garden
postActivitySpots.address: The Old Thomas Telford Centre, Llanfairpwllgwyngyll, LL61 5YF
postActivitySpots.description: A fine dining restaurant in Llanfairpwllgwyngyll serving a multi-course tasting menu featuring local ingredients. A great option for a special occasion.

accommodation.nearestSpot: Close to many spots, 20-30 min drive to Trearddur Bay

accommodation.name: The Boathouse Hotel
accommodation.description: A boutique hotel in Rhoscolyn with stunning sea views. Offers comfortable rooms and a restaurant serving delicious food. Perfect for a relaxing getaway.

accommodation.name: Tyn Lon Camping & Touring Park
accommodation.description: A well-maintained campsite near Rhosneigr. Offers camping pitches and caravan hookups. Conveniently located for exploring the west coast of Anglesey.

accommodation.name: Sandy Mount House
accommodation.description: A stylish hotel and restaurant in Rhosneigr, popular with surfers and beachgoers. Offers comfortable rooms and a lively atmosphere.

accommodation.name: Anglesey Yurts
accommodation.description: Glamping site offering a more unusual stay. Near to several beaches and in a beautiful setting.

events.name: Anglesey Sea Kayak Symposium
events.description: A multi-day event for sea kayakers of all abilities, with coaching, guided trips, and social events. Some overlap with the skills needed for coasteering, such as understanding tides and sea conditions.

discoveredBusinesses.notes: Well-established operator with excellent reviews. Offer guided coasteering experiences around Anglesey.

discoveredBusinesses.description: Cafe located in Trearddur Bay, perfect for a quick bite or drink. A relaxing spot after a session in the sea.

discoveredBusinesses.name: Lobster Pot
discoveredBusinesses.description: A well-known seafood restaurant in Church Bay, perfect for a post-coasteering meal. Famous for lobster and crab.

discoveredBusinesses.name: The White Eagle

discoveredBusinesses.notes: Surf school, worth checking if they offer coasteering or can refer to someone who does.
